items.title: Aquinas offered Five Ways, not one argument

options.text: Five distinct a posteriori arguments in Summa Theologiae I.2.3: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer)

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes a priori arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from a posteriori arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move; an unmoved mover is required. Second Way (efficient causation): a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised separately. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's exchange with Copleston (1948 BBC debate) challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.

items.title: Caste is a complex social hierarchy with religious framings
items.claim: How does the caste system relate to Hindu religion?

options.text: It is purely social with no religious dimension

Varna (the fourfold theoretical division — Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras) is described in the Vedas and the Manusmriti; jati (thousands of birth-based occupational groupings) is the lived reality; modern reform movements (Ambedkar, Gandhi, contemporary Dalit activism) have contested its religious basis
Caste was invented by British colonisers

items.reveal:
The Rig Veda's Purusha Sukta (10.90) describes the four varnas emerging from a cosmic being. The Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE-200 CE) codifies caste duties.

Dalits (formerly 'untouchables') were treated as outside the varna system. B.R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), Dalit leader and chief architect of India's constitution, converted to Buddhism in 1956 partly to escape caste. The Indian Constitution (1950) outlaws untouchability.

The relationship between varna theory and the thousands of jatis on the ground is complex. Caste discrimination persists in many forms — the UK Equality Act 2010 includes caste under race discrimination provisions.
items.why: Religious texts and social systems interact in ways that resist clean separation. The caste case shows how a religious tradition can be deployed for social hierarchy and also generate its own critics.

items.title: The Sunni-Shia split began as a political dispute about succession
items.claim: What is the origin of the Sunni-Shia division?

options.text: Two communities formed in different countries centuries apart

After Muhammad's death in 632 CE, the question of succession divided those who supported Abu Bakr (Sunni) from those who held Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, had been designated (Shia) — fully entrenched after the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala in 680 CE
A modern political invention with no early roots

items.reveal:
Muhammad died on 8 June 632 without naming a successor unambiguously. Abu Bakr was chosen as the first caliph; Ali became fourth caliph (656-661) after the assassinations of Umar and Uthman.

The First Fitna (civil war) and Husayn ibn Ali's death at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) crystallised Shia identity. The annual commemoration of Ashura mourns Husayn.

Today: around 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni, 10-15% Shia. Shia majorities: Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. Significant minorities: Lebanon, Yemen, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India.
items.why: Religious traditions can be deeply shaped by political beginnings. The Sunni-Shia distinction is real and consequential — and originally a question about who should lead, not what to believe.
